abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 10 3 km 2 ), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between “low” and “high” vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South

abstract: Knowledge of how pathogens, in the context of a changing environment, shape the structure of ecological communities remains limited, and little information exists on the ability of small-scale field experiments to predict the consequences of large-scale environmental impacts. We addressed these issues using the emergence of a widespread epidemic (sea star wasting disease, SSWD) on rocky intertidal shorelines. Prior experiments demonstrated strong reductions in sessile species diversity in response to the local experimental removal of the sea star Pisaster ochraceus [R. T. Paine, Am. Nat. 100 , 65–75 (1966); R. T. Paine, Oceologia 15 , 93–120 (1974)] at our site. In surveys of sea star populations over 8 y spanning the onset of the SSWD epidemic, P. ochraceus populations declined by 90%, then subsequently recovered to about one third of pre-epidemic size under an endemic disease phase. Using four different types of temporal data, we documented large increases in populations of the competitively dominant mussel Mytilus californianus following P. ochraceus decline, which were of similar magnitude to those observed in prior field experiments. As in the field experiments, sessile species richness and diversity declined strongly following the onset of the SSWD epidemic as mussels were released from predator control. Our results reveal a strong effect of a pathogen in regulating ecological community structure by disrupting the role of a keystone species, a result anticipated by prior small-scale field experiments.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Field experiments predict ecological response to a large-scale epidemic of an anti-keystone pathogen

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in the social sciences to simulate human behavior and communication, yet validation methods for these applications remain limited. Existing evaluations often rely on human judgments of plausibility, a coarse, difficult-to-scale, and often unreliable benchmark for distinguishing AI-generated from human text. As a result, researchers lack robust tools for assessing the realism of LLM-generated language and for calibrating models to real-world data. We address this gap in two ways. First, we introduce the Conversational Human Authenticity Test (CHAT), a validation framework that combines aggregate metrics of detectability and semantic similarity with interpretable linguistic features, including stylistic markers and topical patterns, to assess how closely LLMs approximate human language in a given dataset. Second, we benchmark nine open-weight LLMs across five calibration strategies, including fine-tuning, stylistic prompting, and context retrieval, on user interactions from X, Bluesky, and Reddit. We find that even after calibration, LLM outputs remain clearly distinguishable from human text, especially in affective tone and emotional expression. Instruction-tuned models generally underperform base models, and larger models do not obviously improve human-likeness. We also identify a trade-off between realism and semantic fidelity: methods that make outputs seem more human often move them further from the content of human responses. Together, these results provide a scalable framework for validation and calibration in LLM-based social simulation while underscoring current limits in reproducing human communication.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: AI-generated language remains systematically distinguishable from human communication

abstract: Modern slavery remains pervasive across many economic sectors. Progress toward eradicating it has been partially hindered by a lack of tested, comprehensive policy responses. Using data on millions of cattle transactions in Brazil, we evaluated how ranchers changed their selling behavior after being added to the "Dirty List," a public registry that names and shames employers found to use modern slavery. Dirty Listed ranchers significantly reduced direct sales to slaughterhouses that signed sustainable supply chain commitments but evaded sanctions by laundering cattle through compliant intermediaries or selling to nonsignatory slaughterhouses. These responses weakened the financial cost of listing to ranchers, and likely allowed beef and leather linked to modern slave labor to enter international supply chains. Our findings highlight the limits of downstream enforcement and underscore the need to monitor upstream suppliers to ensure slavery-free supply chains.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Laundering and evasion in response to antislavery policies in Brazil’s cattle sector

abstract: Chaotic dynamics, commonly seen in weather systems and fluid turbulence, are characterized by their sensitivity to initial conditions, which makes accurate prediction challenging. Recent approaches have focused on developing data-driven models that attempt to preserve invariant statistics over long horizons since many chaotic systems exhibit dissipative behaviors and ergodicity. Despite the recent progress in such models, they are still often prone to generating unbounded trajectories, leading to invalid statistics evaluation. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce a modular framework that provides formal guarantees of trajectory boundedness for neural network chaotic dynamics models. Our core contribution is a dissipative projection layer that leverages control-theoretic principles to ensure the learned system is dissipative. Specifically, our framework simultaneously learns a dynamics emulator and an energy-like function, where the latter is used to construct an algebraic dissipative constraint within the projection layer. Furthermore, the learned invariant level set provides an outer estimate for the system's strange attractor, which is known to be difficult to characterize due to its complex geometry. We demonstrate our model's ability to produce bounded long-horizon forecasts that preserve invariant statistics for chaotic dynamical systems, including Lorenz 96 and a reduced-order model of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Learning dissipative chaotic dynamics with boundedness guarantees

abstract: In mammals, a small population of spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) is established shortly after birth. These cells self-renew and produce sperm for the male's reproductive lifespan, passing the genome on to the next generation. Establishment of a population of SSCs with high genomic integrity is essential. SSCs are derived from a much larger precursor population of male germ cells (MGCs) that differentiate during fetal life. During the last third of gestation, MGCs undergo a prolonged period of G0 cell cycle arrest during which they sustain high levels of transcription and acquire epigenetic programming for SSC fate. Although these differentiation steps can cause cellular and genomic damage, it has been unclear whether selection for germ cell quality occurs during G0 arrest since no classic markers of cell death have been detected. In this study, we used a mouse model to characterize a population of MGCs that begin to accumulate markers of cell death, such as AnnexinV (AnV) and propidium iodide (PI), at E16.5. The AnV- and PI-positive MGC population is characterized by low expression of the RNA-binding protein, Dead End 1, and exhibits dsDNA breaks and mitochondrial dysfunction. Interestingly, we do not see evidence of an active cell death cascade until the time of birth, when phosphorylation of MLKL, a hallmark of necroptotic cell death, occurs. Based on these findings, we propose that variable cellular health is an important basis for selection of SSC precursors.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: In mice, a population of male germ cells shows characteristics of nonapoptotic cell death during G0 arrest

abstract: Metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGlu5) is essential for synaptic plasticity and memory, making it a potential therapeutic target in Alzheimer's disease (AD). While hemispheric asymmetries in hippocampal function have been observed in AD patients, the lateralized contribution of mGlu5 signaling to cognitive decline remains unclear. Here, we show a physiological left-right asymmetry in hippocampal mGlu5 expression in wild-type mice, with higher levels in the left hemisphere, consistent with previous reports. This physiological asymmetry is lost in two distinct mouse models of AD, the J20 and 5xFAD mice, revealing a hemisphere-specific disruption of hippocampal mGlu5 regulation. Using the light-controllable negative allosteric modulator Alloswitch-1, we show that selective inhibition of left, but not right, hippocampal mGlu5 restores working and short-term memory in AD mice. This finding indicates that altered mGlu5 expression does not simply reflect receptor loss, but rather a dysregulated signaling state that remains functionally relevant and pharmacologically targetable. Left-specific modulation also normalizes pathological downstream signaling, including aberrant Pyk2 and GSK-3β activation and tau hyperphosphorylation, across both hemispheres, indicating a widespread impact of hemisphere-selective intervention. These findings establish a functional lateralization of hippocampal mGlu5 signaling and identify the left hippocampus as a critical site for mGlu5-dependent memory dysfunction in AD. They also highlight the therapeutic potential of region-specific photopharmacology for precise intervention in early AD pathology, providing a strategy for spatially targeted modulation of pathological synaptic signaling in neurodegenerative disease.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Shedding light on left hippocampal mGlu5 in Alzheimer’s disease

abstract: Drylands are globally widespread and ecologically important but vulnerable to climate change. Many exhibit spatially self-organized vegetation patterns that enhance resilience by enabling vegetation to reorganize their patterns under drying, thereby optimizing water use and maintaining productivity. Plants can also undergo evolution in response to environmental change. Although both spatial self-organization and rapid evolution are fundamental mechanisms of resilience, their interaction remains largely unknown. Using a theoretical model, we examine how these mechanisms interact to shape vegetation transitions-abrupt or gradual-and ecosystem resilience under climatic drying. We find that pattern formation can suppress adaptation by maintaining soil moisture beneath vegetation patches despite rainfall decline, thereby limiting selection for increased drought tolerance. However, this suppression is largely alleviated under the variable rainfall typical of drylands. In turn, evolution feeds back on self-organization by increasing the spatial plasticity of vegetation patterns and their ability to reorganize under changing climate, although this positive effect weakens as evolutionary rate increases. Considering direct (adaptation) and indirect (pattern-mediated) effects, evolution enhances resilience, with indirect effects via pattern plasticity dominating. Within model scenarios spanning plausible rainfall variability and relative evolutionary-to-ecological rates, more than half of vegetation transitions are abrupt involving biomass losses exceeding 50%, highlighting a potential mechanism underlying recent global observations of widespread abrupt vegetation losses in drylands. These results demonstrate that evolution and spatial self-organization jointly determine dryland resilience under environmental change and highlight the unexpected role of evolution in patterned landscapes, calling for integrative approaches to predict ecosystem responses in a changing world.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Evolution shapes ecosystem resilience through spatial self-organization

abstract: Glaciers populate the mountain ranges of the western conterminous United States and despite their importance to alpine hydrology, their area and volume change have never been comprehensively evaluated. Our study shows that since the mid-twentieth century about one-quarter of the glaciers have disappeared and the overall area and volume are reduced by one-third. The pattern of glacier shrinkage suggests most glaciers in the conterminous United States are largely maintained by local topographic influences due to their small size. These results improve our understanding of evolving high alpine hydrology and importance to ecosystem processes.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Extensive glacier loss in the coterminous United States

abstract: Most stinging animals deliver venom by contracting muscles around a venom reservoir, but honey bees employ a fundamentally different strategy. The stingers of worker bees have the unique ability to autotomize, separating from the body, to continue to sting independently. Despite more than a century of anatomical descriptions, the mechanics of venom pumping have remained unresolved due to the challenges of observing them in action. We recorded high-speed videos of active, autotomized stingers, combined with micro computed tomography-based three-dimensional reconstruction to characterize the biomechanics of stinging in the honey bee Apis mellifera . We reveal that the stinger functions as a unique double-piston micro-pump. Two lancets, each possessing a deformable valve, slide in antiphase within a bulb chamber. These valves dynamically deform to alternately form a seal during the downstroke and collapse during the upstroke, enabling pressure generation for pumping while potentially minimizing backflow during refilling. The inverted tear-drop shape of the bulb facilitates refill even while pumping proceeds. We explored valve deformations and flow behavior by constructing a dynamically scaled physical model of the bulb chamber confirming key features of the pumping cycle and propose mechanisms for valve deformations. The double piston design adds significant design complexity but enables continuous venom delivery in a compact, autonomous unit. These findings provide deeper understanding of venom pumping in honey bees and other Hymenoptera. This study also provides evidence of an axial piston pump within a biological system and offers inspiration for the design of microfluidic pumping devices.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The honey bee stinger: An unusual pump with collapsible double pistons

abstract: Neural circuits establish a stable basal level of synaptic transmission that is maintained throughout life. When synaptic activity is perturbed, homeostatic mechanisms restore this set point, but how neurons reconcile long-term stability and rapid compensatory plasticity remains unclear. Here, we identify two competing presynaptic multimolecular complexes that control steady-state transmission and homeostatic potentiation and define the molecular switch that enables transitions between these functional states. At Drosophila neuromuscular junction, the transmembrane protein PlexinB (PlexB) and the auxiliary subunit Neto-α regulate both basal synaptic function and homeostatic plasticity. PlexB association with presynaptic KaiR1D/Neto-α receptor complexes modulates channel properties and fine-tunes neurotransmitter release, whereas PlexB signaling with Semaphorin2b (Sema2b) and Neto-α drives homeostatic potentiation. KaiR1D and Sema2b/PlexB compete for a limited pool of presynaptic Neto-α. Motor neurons switch from steady-state transmission to homeostatic potentiation by exchanging KaiR1D/Neto-α/PlexB complexes for Neto-α/PlexB/Sema2b. Critically, Neto-α must dissociate from KaiR1D-containing complexes to initiate the homeostatic response. Variants of Neto-α or KaiR1D that fail to dissociate support normal basal neurotransmission but abolish homeostatic plasticity. These findings demonstrate that dynamic reorganization of competing presynaptic protein assemblies enables neurons to preserve stable baseline transmission while mounting robust compensatory responses to perturbations. Given the widespread roles of presynaptic receptors and Semaphorin/Plexin signaling in synaptic regulation, this mechanism may represent a conserved strategy for balancing stability and plasticity in neural circuits.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Competing presynaptic protein assemblies coordinate basal neurotransmission with homeostatic plasticity

abstract: Terrestrial megafauna (animals >1,000 kg) have substantial impacts on ecosystems while alive; yet, we know little about the impacts of these ecosystem engineers after they die. Like whale carcasses in the ocean, terrestrial megacarcasses may leave ecological legacies via the nutrient pulses they create on the landscape. Here, we investigated the impact of elephant megacarcasses on savanna ecosystems in Kruger National Park, South Africa. To determine how elephant carcasses affect below- and aboveground biodiversity and ecosystem processes, we collected soil and plant samples from 40 carcass sites (pairing "on carcass" and "off carcass" samples) ranging from 8 d to 7.7 y postmortem. We found that elephant carcasses released enormous pools of nutrients into savanna soils, increasing ammonium by 31×, nitrate by 7×, and phosphorus by 3× on average. These extreme ammonium concentrations were negatively correlated with the biodiversity of bacteria and plants, which were both suppressed at elephant carcass sites. Despite these decreases in biodiversity, ecosystem processes were strongly elevated at elephant carcass sites, with soil microbial respiration elevated for 1 to 2 y and herbivore grazing >3× higher for 7+ y postmortem. These results demonstrate that elephant megacarcasses generate coldspots of biodiversity but hotspots of ecosystem processes, unveiling a cryptic ecological function of megaherbivores that is extreme in both magnitude and duration relative to carcasses of smaller animals. As humans drive terrestrial megafauna toward extinction, we risk losing not only their ecosystem engineering abilities while they are alive but also the ecological legacies their carcasses create after death.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Nutrient legacies from elephant megacarcasses create coldspots of biodiversity and hotspots of ecosystem processes

abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) is an indirect short-lived climate forcer with uncertainties both in sources and its role in atmospheric oxidation. Based on nine winter-long dual-isotope campaigns at two South Asian receptor sites intercepting the continental outflow, we quantified CO source contributions and emission–sink dynamics. Combustion accounts for 68 to 74% of South Asia regional CO (including 34 to 37% from biomass burning) with secondary atmospheric oxidation contributing 26 to 32% (dominated by oxidation of nonmethane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) at 21 to 26%, with methane oxidation contributing 5.5 to 6.4%). These isotope-observational constraints suggest a twice higher role for atmospheric oxidation than in model estimates. Spatially, the absolute contributions of both primary and secondary CO decrease from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the northern Indian Ocean, while the relative contribution of oxidation-derived CO increases, indicating enhanced secondary CO production near source regions. Observation-model comparison suggests that transport from the continental areas dominates CO over adjacent oceanic regions, with minor local production. During the COVID-19 emission perturbation, combustion-derived CO fell sharply in absolute terms, NMVOC-derived CO rose, and CH 4 -derived CO remained stable, providing an observational constraint on the sensitivity of atmospheric oxidation to emission changes. Our results reveal a significant contribution of CO from atmospheric oxidation in South Asia, calling for a reassessment of regional emission–oxidation coupling in models and of mitigation strategies.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Multiyear dual-isotope fingerprinting at South Asian receptor sites constrains carbon monoxide sources and enhanced oxidation

abstract: Antiferromagnetism and superconductivity are often viewed as competing orders in correlated electron systems. Here, we demonstrate that kinetic frustration in hole motion facilitates their coexistence within the square-lattice repulsive Hubbard model. Combining exact analytical solutions on tailored geometries with large-scale numerical simulations, we reveal a robust pairing mechanism: Holes on opposite sublattices behave as if they carry opposite effective charges due to spin singlet formation from kinetic frustration. This emergent property suppresses phase separation and fosters a coherent [Formula: see text]-wave superconducting channel embedded within a long-range antiferromagnetic background. Our findings establish a minimal yet broadly applicable framework for stabilizing strong-coupling superconductivity in doped Mott insulators.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Antiferromagnetism and tightly bound Cooper pairs induced by kinetic frustration

abstract: Labile zinc ions (Zn 2+ ) are stored in glutamatergic vesicles at specific excitatory synapses in the central nervous system and released into synaptic clefts in an activity-dependent manner. However, the precise roles of synaptic Zn 2+ remain unclear due to a lack of tools capable of analyzing Zn 2+ with synapse-level spatial resolution in vivo. Here, we developed neuroreceptor-based semisynthetic biosensors that function as integrating dosimeters, recording synaptic Zn 2+ by covalent chemistry in the living mouse brain. Using a chemical knock-in strategy, we introduced activity-based Zn 2+ probes with distinct affinities into endogenous α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole-propionic acid or γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors. These in-brain-constructed Zn 2+ sensors enabled region-specific mapping of Zn 2+ in synaptic clefts in the living mouse brain. Imaging-based analyses revealed differences in apparent Zn 2+ levels at excitatory and inhibitory synapses across hippocampal regions during kainate-induced seizures, providing insights into the physiological and pathological functions of synaptic Zn 2+ .
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Imaging and recording of synaptic zinc in the brain by covalent chemistry–based semisynthetic biosensors

abstract: EPSP-spike (E-S) potentiation is a form of plasticity defined by a persistent increase in neuronal spike output for a given synaptic input, reflecting enhanced E-S coupling independent of synaptic strength. However, its cellular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that brief induction of E-S potentiation triggers a sustained calcium activity increase in astrocytes adjacent to the hippocampal CA1 pyramidal layer. Mechanistically, E-S potentiation critically requires GluN2B-containing N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) localized to the neuronal soma. Sustained astrocytic activity promotes E-S potentiation through vesicular release of D-serine, which enhances tonic activation of somatic NMDARs, suppresses A-type potassium currents, and produces a lasting increase in neuronal excitability. Functionally, this astrocyte-dependent E-S potentiation lowers the threshold for subsequent long-term potentiation, conferring a metaplastic influence on hippocampal circuits. These findings identify an astrocyte-neuron signaling mechanism that drives intrinsic plasticity and establish somatic NMDARs as a key site of astrocytic regulation of hippocampal output.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Astrocytic facilitation of somatic NMDARs underpins hippocampal E-S potentiation

abstract: Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of Draxin , which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that Draxin mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3′ untranslated region. We found that Draxin transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of Draxin and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying DDX6 mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of Draxin mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT

abstract: Brain network formation unfolds on a nonuniform developmental timetable, with different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles underpinning the organization of connectomes by creating synthetic networks according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome's topology, operationalized here as the cumulative distributions of network metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography refers to the spatial embedding of the network-the actual anatomical positions of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of individual differences in network formation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Heterochronicity shapes brain network formation

abstract: Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation water has been proposed to be a signature of such hot spots at both the tau fibril-end surface and soluble tau monomers. Although jR2R3-P301L tau exhibits a heterogeneous hydration landscape in its intrinsically disordered state, with enhanced water structuring near the P301L mutation site, it is unclear whether a localized hotspot exists at the fibril end surface and surface water facilitates the initial contacts in templated aggregation. Using rapid 1 H- 15 N SOFAST-HMQC NMR to track seed-induced aggregation of jR2R3-P301L in real time, complemented by molecular dynamics simulation of fibril surface hydration, we identify a residue-specific pinning hotspot that is prone to dewetting followed by sequential folding and incorporation of the remaining segment in a two-step dock-and-lock process. Site-specific spin labeling further demonstrates that blocking this pinning hotspot disrupts templated aggregation, leading to shorter fibrils. The identification of a dominant pinning site will facilitate the rational design of binders to effectively disrupt fibril extension or serve as diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation

abstract: Memory updating promotes cognitive flexibility by enabling suppression of outdated information to optimize behavioral strategies in response to a changing environment. While some circuits involved have been identified, the synaptic mechanisms underlying this process remain uncertain. Here, using a recently developed Kv4.2 knock-in mouse model (Kv4.2TA), we identify a metaplasticity in the hippocampus that accompanies an improvement in cognitive flexibility. Mutation of a C-terminal phosphorylation site (T607) in the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated K + channel protein Kv4.2 drives boosted depotentiation of spike timing-dependent long-term synaptic potentiation mediated by mGluR5 receptors, putative constituents of Kv4.2 macromolecular complexes. We found that mGluR5 receptors are required for the improved cognitive flexibility observed in Kv4.2TA mice. These findings reveal a synaptic correlate associated with memory updating in cognitive flexibility and spotlight the Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex as a therapeutic target for disorders characterized by impairments in cognitive flexibility.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex drives enhanced depotentiation in a mouse model of improved cognitive flexibility

abstract: Efficient immune cell migration requires physical interactions with surrounding tissues. While tissue matrix mechanics influence leukocyte motility, it is unknown how leukocytes exert pushing and pulling forces to traverse cell-dense epithelial tissues in vivo. Here, we leverage the optical transparency of larval zebrafish to identify how physical interactions with epithelial cells regulate mechanisms of neutrophil force generation to navigate cell-dense tissues. Confining forces from epithelial cells induce a mechanosensitive central actin network, mediated by Cdc42 and Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome Protein, which exerts expansile forces on surrounding cells to dilate a path for migration. In concert, direct cell-to-cell (leukocyte-epithelial) contacts mediated by integrin ɑE recognition of epithelial cadherin generate traction forces to enable forward motility. Together, our findings identify how physical interactions with the surrounding cellular environment regulate leukocyte motility through epithelial tissue in vivo.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Direct physical contacts with epithelial cells regulate leukocyte actin dynamics to facilitate intraepithelial motility in vivo

abstract: Evolutionary shape changes of the vertebrate semicircular canals (SCCs) are often ascribed to evolutionary transitions in locomotion, including the origin of flight during the dinosaur-bird transition. However, the potential for transformations of braincase architecture to influence SCC shape independent of sensory-functional adaptation has generally been overlooked. We evaluate the influence of both factors using a large dataset of 146 living and recently extinct crown birds, including taxa representing ~24 independent evolutionary losses of flight, together with Mesozoic stem avialans, nonavialan dinosaurs, and pterosaurs. Among crown birds, evolutionary changes in locomotor capabilities, including the total loss of flight, have only weak effects on SCC shape, contrasting with large effects from changes in braincase geometry. Notably, rotation of the occiput toward a ventral orientation is associated with important changes to SCC shape that match those observed during the dinosaur-bird transition. This suggests that evolutionary transformations of SCC shape during the Mesozoic origin of avian flight resulted from evolutionary changes in the orientation of the craniocervical joint, and not from tuning of SCC sensory function. These findings illuminate the importance of integrated morphological changes to the head-neck system during bird origins and challenge the long-standing assumption that SCC morphology enables confident inferences of the locomotor capabilities of extinct vertebrates.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Coordinated transformations of the labyrinth and occiput during the dinosaur–bird transition

abstract: The axon initial segment (AIS), situated within the first 20 to 60 µm of the axon, is essential for action potential generation and maintenance of axonal identity [M. N. Rasband, Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 11 , 552–562 (2010)]. Its structure relies on the beta (β)-IV-spectrin/AnkyrinG (AnkG) scaffold arranged periodically underneath the plasma membrane, harboring diverse membrane proteins [K. Xu, G. Zhong, X. Zhuang, Science 339 , 452–456 (2013); K. L. Hedstrom, Y. Ogawa, M. N. Rasband, J. Cell Biol. 183 , 635–640 (2008)]. Although a ~190-nm cytoskeletal periodic organization is well established, the precise stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of AIS proteins within the ~190-nm spatial period remain rudimentary, mostly for lack of sufficient spatial resolution and labeling efficiency. Here, using expansion microscopy and cryoelectron tomography, which overcome these technical limitations, we present data on the organization of the AnkG-associated complex within the ~190-nm spatial period. We demonstrate that exactly two AnkG molecules are situated within each period and with their C termini separated by ~80 nm. By contrast, the AnkG-associated cell-adhesion protein neurofascin-186 appears in clusters of varying sizes that are consistent with the periodic organization of AnkG pairs, yet suggesting a more complex molecular arrangement between the two molecules. Altogether, our approach provides insights into AIS molecular organization and protein stoichiometry.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Double periodicity of the AnkyrinG-associated complex in the axon initial segment

abstract: Simulations of the ocean wave climate are critical for assessment of coastal processes and hazards in observation sparse regions such as the Arctic. While the multidecade wind and ice datasets necessary for driving long-term wave simulations have proven reliable for such efforts, the presence of landfast ice along shorelines at scales not represented by these data has been a persistent uncertainty impeding accurate analysis of impacts to Arctic coasts. Here, we explore this uncertainty by producing a historical high-resolution wave simulation and combining simulation outputs with landfast ice data for the Alaskan Arctic. The resulting dataset yields an improved assessment of coastal waves and identifies stark contrasts in the seasonal wave exposure of the Chukchi and Beaufort regions. Notably, analysis shows that absent supplemented landfast ice, coastal ice cover is broadly underestimated by 10 to 25 d, resulting in wave energy being overestimated by 5 to 10% in shallow depths nearshore. Notably, these figures can reach up to 70 d of underestimation for ice cover and 48% overestimation of wave energy in certain locations. The persistent overestimation and potential for extreme positive biases in coastal wave assessment highlight the need for representation of landfast ice in Arctic coastal analysis efforts and our analysis reveals the spatial and temporal biases for related research.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Improved assessment of Alaskan Arctic coastal wave exposure accounting for landfast ice

abstract: Heme crystallization is central to malaria parasites’ survival during the erythrocytic stage of the disease, yet how clinically relevant antimalarial drugs modulate this process at the molecular level remains unclear. Here we employ stage-resolved parasite assays and multiscale in vitro approaches to explore the interactions between lumefantrine (LF), one of the popular components of current combination therapies, and hematin crystallization. Pulse LF suppresses Plasmodium falciparum during both ring and trophozoite stages. Under biomimetic conditions, LF markedly reduces β-hematin crystal growth rates. High-resolution atomic force microscopy reveals that individual LF molecules bind directly to crystal steps, physically constraining step motion through a previously unreported step-capping mechanism. This localized inhibition propagates to the mesoscale, producing step broadening, reduced interstep spacing, and causing surface kinetic roughening. In contrast to its strong inhibition of crystal growth, LF enhances hematin nucleation by promoting the formation of mesoscopic hematin-rich clusters, as detected by a combination of scattering and microscopy techniques. Attachment of the nucleated crystallites to larger crystal surfaces initiates a nonclassical inhibition sequence by straining the crystal interface, which further impedes step growth.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A multiscale framework for heme crystallization inhibition: From single-molecule step-capping to parasite suppression

abstract: The origin and early radiation of winged insects (Pterygota) represent one of the most transformative events in terrestrial evolution, yet phylogenetic relationships among their basalmost lineages (Ephemeroptera, Odonata and Neoptera) continue to be a central debate within insect systematics. Here, we present the most taxonomically comprehensive phylogenomic analysis to date, leveraging genomic and transcriptomic data from 101 species, including 16 sequenced ephemeropteran genomes. Employing 1,367 universal single-copy orthologs across two supermatrices, we used concatenation- and coalescent-based frameworks under homogeneous and heterogeneous, and multispecies coalescent models. Our analyses support Palaeoptera monophyly. Although coalescent-based methods initially suggested a Chiastomyaria (Ephemeroptera + Neoptera) topology, subsequent signal dissection and topology tests confirm that the preponderance of genomic signal favors a monophyletic Palaeoptera. Furthermore, we identify incomplete lineage sorting and gene tree estimation error as the primary drivers of previous topological conflicts. Our molecular dating results point to an Early Devonian origin of crown-Pterygota, whereas crown-Palaeoptera first emerged in the Late Devonian. By reconciling molecular evidence with morphological synapomorphies, such as wing-base sclerite homologies, this study provides a coherent framework for the early evolution of winged insects, supports a single origin of wings, and identifies the neopteran wing-folding mechanism as a singular evolutionary innovation.

journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Phylogenomics confirms Palaeoptera monophyly and illuminates the origin of winged insects

abstract: CO 2 transporters enable bacterial CO 2 -concentrating mechanisms by catalyzing directional hydration of CO 2 , yet the basis of this vectorial carbonic anhydrase (CA) activity remains an open question. We used cryoelectron microscopy to determine the structure of the DAB1 complex from Thermocrinis albus to 2.29 Å, revealing a heterotrimer in which a deeply buried β-CA active site in DabA is structurally coupled to the proton-translocating subunit DabB. Two conformational states define distinct solvent channels for substrate entry and product exit. A suppressor screen identifies mutations that disrupt coupling while retaining CA activity, underlying the importance of conserved residues that link proton translocation to active-site remodeling. These results support a model in which proton-driven conformational changes regulate substrate access to the active site, enabling vectorial CO 2 hydration.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO 2 uptake by DAB1

abstract: We study how kinship and reciprocity shape giving and child care support in societies with limited access to markets. Extending Hamilton's rule to incorporate reciprocity, we test it using behavioral data from dictator games and surveys in remote matrilocal and patrilocal villages of northeast India (N = 406 parents of young children). We replicate with data from urban Manila neighborhoods (N = 301) and the Solomon Islands (N = 624). Consistent with predictions, transfers to recipients increase with genetic relatedness to the donor and even more with relatedness to the donor's child-a hallmark of reciprocity anchored in shared genetic investment. Nonanonymous conditions amplify giving, especially to nonkin. Cultural norms shape cooperation, but do not trump genetic relatedness. These results underscore the role of affinal ties and reciprocal exchange in sustaining cooperation, and suggest a mechanism through which cooperative breeding could contribute to the emergence of generalized reciprocity and human sociality.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Integrating cooperative breeding with reciprocity and culture extends Hamilton’s rule to humans

abstract: Single-crystal materials are essential for fundamental catalysis studies and advanced technologies; however, synthesizing single crystals that simultaneously integrate mesoporosity, tunable size, and well-defined surfaces remains challenging. Here, we report a wet-chemical, template-free strategy to synthesize mesoporous quasi-single-crystal CeO 2 superparticles (SPs). Operando wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering combined with theoretical modeling reveal a nonclassical growth mechanism driven by the oriented attachment of nanocluster building blocks. This process yields high-surface-area quasi-single crystals that preferentially expose energetically favorable (111) facets on both the external surfaces and internal pore walls, thereby enhancing the stabilization of active sites when used as heterogeneous catalyst supports. Using this approach, we demonstrate broad applicability by synthesizing highly dispersed precious metal–loaded CeO 2 (M/CeO 2 , M = Pd, Pt, Rh, or Ir) and metal-doped CeO 2 (Cu–CeO 2 ) SPs. Moreover, Pd/CeO 2 SPs exhibit effective stabilization of Pd clusters in CO 2 hydrogenation to methanol, delivering a high methanol selectivity of 85% and markedly improved durability compared with conventional supports.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Nonclassical growth to mesoporous quasi-single crystal CeO 2 superstructures with a well-defined surface

abstract: Atmospheric new particle formation (NPF) has been observed across virtually all tropospheric environments, yet the meteorological conditions that favor or suppress it have resisted clear theoretical resolution. Here we show that, for neutral chemistries in which a strongly bound molecular pair constitutes the critical cluster, the thermodynamic precondition for NPF is set by a single quantity: the effective binding free energy of that pair, Δ G AB ° ( T , RH ) , which captures the competing influences of temperature and relative humidity in a closed-form analytical framework. Applied to the sulfuric acid–dimethylamine system in the boundary layer, the theory reproduces observed clustering across laboratory experiments and field campaigns spanning a polluted megacity, a remote high-altitude site, and an ultra-pristine boreal peatland, all without kinetic fitting parameters; precursor concentrations and the condensation sink enter as separable factors that govern the subsequent production rate. The framework reveals an optimal Δ G AB ° that maximizes cluster production, providing a thermodynamic basis for why NPF peaks at midday, favors spring over other seasons, occurs under heat wave conditions despite temperatures approaching + 40 ° C, and can even arise on rare evenings in near-pristine conditions. More broadly, the theory exposes the inherent relationship between atmospheric conditions and the earliest steps of particle formation, offering a general interpretive tool that complements and extends what observations and simulations alone cannot provide.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Thermodynamic origin of atmospheric new particle formation: Theory for stable nucleating pairs

abstract: Bacteria of the human microbiota encode an abundance of natural products that likely mediate bacterial competition, local colonization patterns, and human health and disease. However, very few of these compounds have been identified and characterized to date. During our investigation of Streptococcus mitis , an important early colonizer of the oral cavity, we identified and structurally characterized a family of peptide natural products, termed miranthins herein, that contain an unusual macrocycle formed by an Asp-Cys β-carbon thioether crosslink. We determined that the most abundantly secreted miranthin is a “Trojan horse” antibiotic that enters sensitive cells via the Ami oligopeptide transporter, is hydrolyzed and activated by aminopeptidase N, and subsequently inhibits ribosomal translation to curb the growth of streptococcal competitors. The miranthins are narrow-spectrum antibiotics that could enable S. mitis to modulate community dynamics in the oral cavity, highlighting the importance of peptide natural products in interspecies competition in the microbiome.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Discovery and characterization of miranthins, “Trojan horse” antibiotic modulators of bacterial composition in the oral microbiome

abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often found forming a peripheral stromal barrier around tumors. Here, this paradigm is challenged using microfabricated 3D cancer-CAF spheroid models combined with quantitative magnetic force tensiometry. A surface tension atlas is established for eight cancer cell lines, three CAF populations, and heterotypic tumor-CAF assemblies, spanning nearly two orders of magnitude. Surface tension is first shown to govern spheroid morphology and modulate drug response. Besides, CAFs consistently occupy the highest end of the surface tension hierarchy, predicting core rather than peripheral localization and directly challenging the shell paradigm. Yet confocal imaging reveals not only central accumulation but also complete CAF-tumor mixing, including in spheroids where cancer cells exhibit surface tensions nearly two orders of magnitude lower than CAFs. Surface tension alone therefore fails to predict CAF organization. Instead, the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) state of cancer cells emerges as a major determinant: epithelial-like tumors promote CAF core accumulation, whereas mesenchymal-like states favor persistent mixing. Peripheral CAF localization emerges only under restricted conditions combining high tumor cohesion and sequential stromal recruitment. Together, these results identify surface tension, EMT state, and assembly chronology as joint determinants of tumor-stroma architecture, revealing a context-dependent organization landscape rather than a universal CAF shell.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Cell identity competes with surface tension to determine stromal organization in tumor spheroids beyond the CAF shell paradigm

abstract: The abiotic emergence of ribonucleosides remains a central challenge in origin-of-life research because ribonucleosides form inefficiently and are often unstable under prebiotically plausible conditions. Here we show that interfacial microenvironments within aqueous micro- and nanoscale compartments containing D-ribose, phosphoric acid, and nucleobases promote ribonucleoside formation by creating reaction-permissive physicochemical conditions independent of the specific compartment type. Across a diverse range of compartmentalized systems, including gas–oil–water micro/nanobubbles, gas–water micro/nanobubbles, microscale lipid-bilayer vesicles, and oil–water emulsion systems, ribonucleosides form abiotically in the absence of enzymatic catalysis. Under selected interfacial conditions, multiple ribonucleosides, including cytidine, are generated without added catalysts. Comparison among these systems reveals that interfacial architecture and coupled physicochemical properties strongly influence both reaction efficiency and product stability. CO 2 -based micro/nanobubbles support sustained cytidine accumulation, highlighting the importance of coupled gas–liquid and liquid–liquid interfaces. Ribonucleoside synthesis also depends on compartment size, whereas variations in oil content within micro/nanobubbles selectively modulate inosine formation, underscoring the sensitivity of nucleoside chemistry to interfacial properties. These findings identify interfacial microenvironments within micro- and nanoscale compartments as a general physical framework for ribonucleoside emergence and suggest that ubiquitous compartmentalized interfaces on early Earth could have provided robust settings for prebiotic ribonucleoside chemistry.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Interfacial microenvironments enable abiotic ribonucleoside formation in micro- and nanoscale compartments
